summary: Paul addresses doubters in Corinth who deny resurrection. He argues Christ was truly raised, listing eyewitnesses, then says if Christ wasn't raised, Christian faith is empty. He explains resurrection body like seed to plant, and ends with triumph: death swallowed in victory, therefore keep laboring.
whyItMatters: This is the earliest and most detailed argument for resurrection, written 20-25 years after Jesus' death, citing eyewitnesses still alive. It frames resurrection not as myth but as bodily, historical, and central — without it, Christianity collapses; with it, everything changes.

context.author: Paul
context.audience: Christians in Corinth — Greek port city, status obsessed, influenced by philosophy that devalued body
context.setting: Corinthian doubts about afterlife; some said resurrection already happened spiritually or doesn't happen
context.literaryForm: Letter — argument with eyewitness list, analogies, and pastoral climax

outline.heading: Gospel received: Christ died and rose according to Scriptures
outline.note: Includes early creed and eyewitness list

outline.heading: If no resurrection, faith is vain
Christ firstfruits, then those who are his, in order
Why be baptized for dead? Why suffer?
outline.note: Hard verses — Paul cites Corinthian practice he may not endorse

outline.heading: What kind of body? Seed analogy
Victory over death — how to live now

keyVerses.text: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures
keyVerses.why: Early creed Paul received, dated within 2-5 years of crucifixion, core gospel summary.

keyVerses.text: If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith also is in vain.
keyVerses.why: Paul makes resurrection falsifiable — admits if false, his mission is pointless.

keyVerses.text: Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?
keyVerses.why: Triumphant taunt from Hosea and Isaiah, climax of argument.

questions.question: Why does Paul list eyewitnesses like Cephas and 500 people?
questions.answer: Greco-Roman courts valued eyewitnesses. Paul names individuals still alive in AD 55 (20 years after), inviting verification: 'go ask them.' The 500 is a large group, reducing hallucination explanation. Cephas is Peter's Aramaic name.

questions.question: What does 'according to the Scriptures' mean?
questions.answer: Not just that it fulfills prophecy, but that it fits the pattern of Scripture — Passover lamb dies to save, third day motif (Hosea 6:2, Jonah). Early Christians read resurrection as climax of Israel's story, not isolated miracle.

questions.question: What is baptism for the dead in verse 29? Is that a practice we should do?
questions.answer: Hardest verse in chapter. Some in Corinth were baptized on behalf of deceased relatives. Paul doesn't command it; he uses it as an argument: if dead aren't raised, why are people doing this? He cites their practice to show inconsistency, not endorsement. Meaning is debated.

questions.question: What kind of body is resurrection body? Ghost or physical?
questions.answer: Paul says not ghost, not same as now, but not unrelated — like seed vs plant: continuity (same organism) and discontinuity (very different). He says perishable to imperishable, dishonorable to glorious, weak to powerful — transformed physicality, not ethereal spirit. Greeks thought body bad, spirit good; Paul says body matters.

questions.question: Why does Paul say 'flesh and blood cannot inherit kingdom' if resurrection is bodily?
questions.answer: Flesh and blood here means mortal, perishable existence in present corruption, not materiality itself. He says this mortal must put on immortality — transformed, not discarded.

questions.question: What does 'firstfruits' mean?
questions.answer: In harvest, firstfruits are first sheaf offered, guaranteeing rest of harvest coming and same quality. Christ as firstfruits means his resurrection is prototype and guarantee of others, same kind of body to follow.

questions.question: How does this chapter end with practical application?
questions.answer: After dense argument, Paul says: because resurrection is true, your labor is not in vain (v58). If death wins, nothing matters. If resurrection wins, everyday faithful work — preaching, serving, enduring — has lasting significance.

glossary.def: First portion of harvest offered, guaranteeing rest of crop of same kind.
Realm of the dead in Greek thought; sometimes translated hell or grave.
Aramaic name for Peter, meaning Rock.
